meta.label: Period products
meta.attribution: Curated from public materials, certifications, product pages, B Corp profiles, and reusable-vs-single-use LCA/safety references - not medical advice. Comfort, access, fit, disability, flow, dysphoria, infection history, and safe-use guidance matter more than any score. Always follow product instructions and clinical safety guidance. Reviewed 2026-06. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: Menstrual cup (e.g. DivaCup, Saalt)

environment.note: Carbon Literacy's 2025 summary says one year of menstrual-cup use has under 1.5% of disposable products' environmental impact.

health.note: FDA's 2025 draft guidance covers menstrual cups in updated testing and labeling recommendations; correct cleaning and instructions still matter.

economical.note: Carbon Literacy's 2025 summary cites menstrual-cup use at about 10% of disposable-product cost over one year and 5% over ten years.

ethics.note: Saalt is a Certified B Corp and reports a revenue-linked period-care access and education impact program.

accessibility.note: Cups and discs are widely sold but have a learning curve, fit variation, and cleaning needs.

products.description: A reusable internal cup can be the lowest-waste and lowest-long-run-cost option when it fits the user and cleaning routine.

products.name: Reusable cloth pads

environment.note: Carbon Literacy's 2025 summary names cloth pads among reusable options that can last years and reduce waste and long-term costs.

health.note: Reusable pad products can use organic cotton and avoid internal wear; users still need washing/drying hygiene.

economical.note: Reusable pads have higher upfront prices, but current reusable-product summaries emphasize multi-year use and lower long-term costs.

ethics.note: Aisle is a Certified B Corp with a long-running inclusive reusable-period-care mission.

accessibility.note: Requires laundering, drying space, and carrying used pads; easier online than in many local stores.

products.description: Washable cloth pads avoid internal insertion and reduce single-use waste, but require laundering and upfront purchase.

products.name: Menstrual disc

environment.note: Reusable discs use the same reuse logic as cups: durable internal collection instead of monthly disposables.

health.note: Saalt Disc is described as medical-grade silicone, BPA-free and latex-free; safe use still depends on fit and instructions.

economical.note: Reusable discs have upfront cost but can last for years, reducing repeat tampon/pad purchases.

ethics.note: Saalt provides a B Corp/impact example in reusable cups and discs, but the broader disc market varies.

accessibility.note: State health explainer describes reusable discs as sustainable but internal and placement-dependent, so the learning curve remains real.

products.description: Reusable menstrual discs can offer cup-like waste savings with a different fit, but they remain newer and fit-sensitive.

products.name: Period underwear (WUKA, Modibodi…)

environment.note: WUKA markets period pants as reusable replacements for disposable pads and tampons, reducing single-use waste.

health.note: ACS's 2025 research update found some reusable period underwear and pads contained PFAS, so brand-level material disclosure and recent testing matter.

economical.note: Higher upfront price can pay back through repeated use if the garment fits and lasts.

ethics.note: Reusable-underwear makers vary; WUKA publishes materials/sustainability claims but this generic category should be checked brand by brand.

accessibility.note: Underwear format is intuitive and increasingly available, but fit, absorbency, washing, and upfront cost can limit access.

products.description: Reusable absorbent underwear is easy to use and lower waste, but PFAS/testing transparency varies by brand.

products.name: Organic cotton tampons/pads (Natracare, TOTM)

environment.note: Natracare sells plastic-free and compostable/biodegradable organic cotton tampon formats, though still single-use.

health.note: Natracare uses 100% GOTS-certified organic cotton and publishes certification/testing claims; this is materials transparency, not medical superiority.

economical.note: Organic disposables usually cost more per cycle than basic conventional disposables or long-lived reusables.

ethics.note: MADE SAFE notes Natracare claims are validated by independent accreditations including Soil Association Organic, GOTS, and Plastic-Free.

accessibility.note: Natracare and similar organic disposables are available online and in many natural/supermarket channels, but not everywhere.

products.description: Organic cotton disposable pads and tampons improve materials transparency and reduce plastic in some formats, but they remain single-use.

products.name: Organyc organic cotton tampons/pads

environment.note: Organyc's no-applicator tampons are 100% biodegradable and avoid applicator plastic, but they are still single-use.

health.note: Organyc says the tampons are 100% certified organic cotton with no chlorine bleach, latex, parabens, perfumes, or super-absorbent powders.

economical.note: Organic disposable tampons and pads remain recurring purchases and usually cost more per cycle than basic store-brand options.

ethics.note: The product page displays GOTS Certified Organic, ICEA, and Vegan OK signals, but no B Corp-style governance certification was found.

accessibility.note: Sold online and through some US retail channels, but less universally available than mainstream Tampax, Always, or store-brand products.

products.description: Organyc is a practical organic-cotton disposable option, strongest when no-applicator tampons or certified cotton matter more than reusability.

products.name: Aisle reusable pads & underwear

environment.note: Aisle makes reusable pads and underwear intended to replace disposable pads and liners.

health.note: Aisle product pages emphasize organic cotton gussets and reusable cloth formats; users still need laundering and fit care.

economical.note: Reusable pads/underwear cost more upfront but are designed for repeated cycle use rather than monthly replacement.

ethics.note: B Lab describes Aisle as a category-defining, size- and gender-inclusive reusable period-care B Corp.

accessibility.note: Online-first model and upfront price limit instant access, while inclusive sizing improves fit access.

products.description: Aisle is a mature reusable-period-care brand with strong B Corp credentials, inclusive sizing, and organic-cotton product design.

products.name: DAME reusable tampon applicator

environment.note: DAME reusable applicator is designed to replace disposable tampon applicators while still using non-applicator tampons.

health.note: Product is marketed as medical-grade and self-sanitising; hygiene depends on following cleaning instructions.

economical.note: Upfront applicator cost plus ongoing tampon costs means savings are smaller than cups/pads but better than buying applicators every cycle.

ethics.note: B Lab lists DAME/Sanitary Owl as a B Corp giving 10% of profits to charity and focused on sustainable period products.

accessibility.note: Mostly UK/online and requires comfort with applicator cleaning and non-applicator tampons.

products.description: A reusable applicator lowers plastic applicator waste for tampon users, but still depends on ongoing tampon purchases and cleaning comfort.

products.name: Cora organic cotton pads/tampons

environment.note: Single-use products, but Cora organic lines use organic cotton and publish reusable options too.

health.note: Retail listings describe Cora pads/tampons as organic-cotton, fragrance-free/dye-free options; this is materials transparency, not a medical claim.

economical.note: Premium organic disposable pricing remains a recurring cost compared with reusables or store brands.

ethics.note: Cora says each purchase supports period products and body-literacy resources for people who might otherwise go without.

accessibility.note: US direct, subscription, and major retail availability make it easier to find than many boutique organic brands.

products.description: Cora is a premium organic-cotton disposable brand with strong access-giving claims and US retail reach.

products.name: TOTM organic & reusable period care

environment.note: TOTM offers organic cotton disposables plus reusable period-care options, so impact varies by product choice.

health.note: TOTM states pads are made with 100% organic GOTS-certified cotton and plastic-free packaging.

economical.note: Organic disposables are premium recurring purchases; reusable options have higher upfront cost.

ethics.note: B Lab lists TOTM as a Certified B Corp focused on menstrual wellbeing, dignity, and sustainable organic/reusable products.

accessibility.note: UK/EU online and retail availability is decent, but global reach is lower than mainstream disposables.

products.description: TOTM combines certified organic cotton disposables with reusable options and B Corp accountability, strongest in UK/EU channels.

products.name: August organic cotton pads/tampons

environment.note: August states products use 100% organic cotton and compostable wrappers for pads, but pads/tampons remain single-use.

health.note: Brand states 100% organic cotton with no dyes or fragrances; this is materials transparency, not medical advice.

economical.note: Target listings show premium per-count pricing compared with basic store-brand tampons/pads.

ethics.note: August impact page states a mission around sustainable, traceable period products and period-stigma reduction.

accessibility.note: US online, subscription, and Target retail availability improves access versus online-only organic brands.

products.description: August offers organic cotton pads and tampons with strong youth/period-access messaging and growing US retail availability.

products.name: Hey Girls period care

environment.note: Hey Girls offers reusable pads, pants, and cups that it says last 5-10 years, plus plant-based disposable products.

health.note: Hey Girls says its disposables use 100% certified organic cotton, bamboo and corn starch, with natural materials and no hidden chlorine or toxins.

economical.note: Reusable products can lower long-run costs, while disposable and subscription products remain recurring purchases.

ethics.note: Hey Girls says it is a social enterprise donating 100% of profit to fighting period poverty, with a buy one, donate one model and 42 million products donated by November 2024.

accessibility.note: Strong UK institutional/public-sector access and direct shopping, but less global retail reach than mainstream disposable brands.

products.description: Hey Girls is a UK social-enterprise period-care range with reusables, organic disposables, and unusually concrete period-poverty work.

products.name: Saalt cups, discs & period underwear

environment.note: Saalt's core range is reusable cups, discs, and leakproof underwear rather than monthly disposable pads/tampons.

health.note: Saalt states its cups are medical-grade silicone, BPA-free, and made without PFAS; safe use still depends on cleaning and fit.

economical.note: Reusable cups/discs have a higher upfront price but replace many cycles of disposable products if they fit the user.

ethics.note: Saalt is a Certified B Corp and reports period-care access and education programs through its impact work.

accessibility.note: Saalt sells direct and through major US retail channels, but internal reusables still have a learning curve.

products.description: Saalt is a recognizable B Corp reusable-period-care brand with cups, discs, underwear, and stronger access programs than most boutique reusables.

products.name: DIVA Cup

environment.note: DIVA Cup is a reusable menstrual cup, avoiding recurring tampon/pad waste when it works for the user.

health.note: DIVA states the cup is 100% medical-grade silicone with no added BPA, latex, dyes, or plastics.

economical.note: DIVA says its cup can be used for several years with proper care, reducing repeat disposable purchases.

ethics.note: B Lab lists Diva International as a Certified B Corp with period-care education, donation, and research work.

accessibility.note: DIVA is sold direct and through major retail, but cups remain fit- and comfort-dependent.

products.description: DIVA is a long-running reusable cup brand with unusually strong B Corp accountability and mainstream retail familiarity.

products.name: Mooncup

environment.note: Mooncup is a reusable menstrual cup brand built around replacing disposable period products and reducing plastic.

health.note: B Lab notes Mooncup launched the world's first medical-grade silicone menstrual cup in 2002 and emphasizes no plastic or irritants.

economical.note: Reusable-cup economics are strong when fit works, but the upfront purchase can be wasted if the cup does not suit the user.

ethics.note: Mooncup is a Certified B Corp with an overall B Impact Score of 147.5.

accessibility.note: Strong UK/EU brand recognition and online availability, but internal cups still require fit, comfort, and cleaning access.

products.description: Mooncup adds a UK/EU reusable-cup anchor: high on waste reduction and ethics, still dependent on fit and comfort.

products.name: Ruby Cup

environment.note: Ruby Cup sells reusable cups and period underwear, and says a treated cup can last up to 10 years.

health.note: Ruby Cup positions its cup as a soft reusable internal product; safe use still depends on cleaning, fit, and user comfort.

economical.note: The reuse model can reduce repeat disposable spending, though the UK online price is a meaningful upfront cost.

ethics.note: Ruby Cup reports 155,000+ cups donated and a Buy One Give One model for people without access to safe period products.

accessibility.note: Ruby Cup ships internationally but is more online/UK-centered than large US retail period brands.

products.description: Ruby Cup is a reusable cup and period-underwear brand with a concrete donation model, strongest for shoppers who value period-equity impact.

products.name: WUKA period pants

environment.note: B Lab says one pair of WUKA period pants can save 200 single-use disposables from landfill/ocean pollution.

health.note: WUKA sells reusable leakproof underwear; as with all period underwear, brand-level PFAS/testing transparency still matters.

economical.note: Reusable underwear costs more upfront but can replace many disposable pad or tampon purchases if absorbency and fit work.

ethics.note: WUKA is a Certified B Corp and B Lab describes it as the UK's first period-wear brand.

accessibility.note: WUKA has UK/EU strength and online global visibility, but upfront price, sizing, washing, and drying needs can limit access.

products.description: WUKA is a B Corp period-underwear specialist with strong waste-reduction claims, best when the user's fit, washing, and budget constraints line up.

products.name: The Period Company underwear

environment.note: Period. describes its underwear as non-disposable and reusable, avoiding ongoing tampon and pad waste.

health.note: Period. says its underwear is made without PFAS and has UL 'PFAS NOT DETECTED' validation for all products.

economical.note: Period. claims five pairs cost about $60 per year and can last 2-10 years depending on care, compared with recurring disposables.

ethics.note: The brand offers broad sizing and adaptable underwear, but no B Corp-style third-party governance certification was found.

accessibility.note: Sizes run XS to 6X and the brand ships worldwide, making reusable underwear more accessible than many premium period-underwear brands.

products.description: The Period Company is a lower-cost reusable-underwear option with broad sizing and PFAS-not-detected validation, though less formal certification than B Corp peers.

products.name: Rael organic pads & tampons

environment.note: Rael organic pad and tampon lines improve material signals, but most formats still include single-use wrappers, cores, applicators, or backings.

health.note: Rael tampons use a certified organic cotton core and avoid synthetic fragrances, dyes, and harsh chemicals.

economical.note: Organic disposable period care remains a recurring purchase and usually costs more than basic store brands.

ethics.note: Rael says its period products are cruelty-free, but it lacks the stronger B Corp-style governance signal of some peers.

accessibility.note: Rael is available direct and through major US retailers, making organic disposable options comparatively easy to find.

products.description: Rael makes organic-material disposable pads and tampons easy to find in US retail, though the format remains recurring and mostly single-use.

products.name: The Honey Pot period care

environment.note: Honey Pot pads and tampons are mostly disposable; organic cotton covers/cores help materials but do not remove single-use waste.

health.note: Honey Pot discloses herbal and non-herbal options; essential-oil cooling can be welcome for some users and irritating for others.

economical.note: Premium retail period products are a recurring purchase, though they are often cheaper upfront than reusable underwear or cups.

ethics.note: Honey Pot states its products are cruelty-free and built around plant-derived feminine care.

accessibility.note: Broad Walmart/major-retail availability makes the brand easier to access than many boutique organic period lines.

products.description: The Honey Pot is a high-access plant-derived period-care brand; its herbal pads are useful to name because the cooling ingredients are not for everyone.

products.name: Flex Reusable Disc

environment.note: Reusable disc designed to last for years and replace hundreds of disposable products, but it still requires washing and fit success.

health.note: Flex states the reusable disc is 100% medical-grade silicone, ISO 10993 tested, and not made with BPA, phthalates, or natural rubber latex.

economical.note: Higher upfront price than a box of disposables, but reusable design and HSA/FSA eligibility improve long-run value.

ethics.note: A scaled period-care startup with strong product transparency, but no B Corp or comparable mission certification found.

accessibility.note: One of the most visible reusable-disc brands in the US, with beginner-friendly design claims and direct online purchase.

products.description: Flex makes the reusable-disc format more mainstream and approachable, with good material disclosure and a still-real insertion/removal learning curve.

products.name: nixit menstrual disc

environment.note: Reusable, plastic-free disc intended to replace ongoing pad and tampon purchases, though washing and sterilizing are required.

health.note: nixit states the disc is 100% medical-grade silicone, BPA-free, FDA registered, Health Canada authorized, and made in Canada.

economical.note: The brand positions nixit as a one-time reusable purchase that can save repeated disposable-product costs.

ethics.note: Good materials disclosure and Canadian manufacturing signal quality, but no broad third-party mission certification was found.

accessibility.note: Online-first and one-size design reduce some choice friction, but price and disc fit still make access uneven.

products.description: nixit is a higher-capacity reusable disc with strong material disclosure, best for users who want a suction-free internal option.

products.name: Lunette Period Cup

environment.note: Lunette says one cup can last up to 10 years and replace thousands of disposable pads and tampons.

health.note: Product page states 100% soft medical-grade silicone and no unwanted chemicals detected; safe use still depends on cleaning and instructions.

economical.note: Typical cup pricing is higher upfront but strong over years when fit and care work for the user.

ethics.note: Long-running reusable brand with sustainability and charity pages, but not a B Corp-style governance certification.

accessibility.note: Available through Lunette's global store and retail channels, though cup fit and cleaning needs remain access barriers.

products.description: Lunette is a long-established cup option with strong reusability and material claims, useful as a recognizable European cup benchmark.

products.name: Modibodi period underwear

environment.note: Modibodi frames its leak-proof garments as reusable apparel for repeated period and leak management.

health.note: Modibodi states it does not intentionally use PFAS or nanotechnology and that all products are OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified.

economical.note: Reusable underwear has a higher upfront cost than pads, but repeated wear can reduce long-run disposable purchases if the garment lasts.

ethics.note: The support center cites social-impact and sustainability work, but the brand is not scored like a mission-locked B Corp.

accessibility.note: Wide style and absorbency range, including teen and heavy options, makes the format easier to match to real use than many niche brands.

products.description: Modibodi is a mainstream reusable-underwear option with useful PFAS/OEKO-TEX disclosure and broad absorbency choices.

products.name: Thinx period underwear

environment.note: Reusable leakproof underwear can reduce disposable pad/tampon use, but product and laundering impacts remain.

health.note: Thinx's 2023 settlement covered PFAS and marketing allegations while denying wrongdoing; current safety page says PFAS are not part of product design.

economical.note: More expensive upfront than pads, but reusable underwear can pay back over repeated cycles if it fits and holds up.

ethics.note: PFAS-related marketing settlement makes trust weaker than brands with cleaner third-party certification histories.

accessibility.note: Very recognizable US reusable-underwear brand with multiple period, teen, and leakproof styles online.

products.description: Thinx belongs in the lens because many people know it; the reusable convenience is real, and so are the PFAS-related trust concerns.

products.name: L. organic period care

environment.note: Organic cotton helps the materials story, but L. pads and tampons remain single-use and include plastic/polymer components by format.

health.note: L. discloses tampon and pad ingredients and says tampons use US-grown organic cotton core fibers without fragrances, rayon, or synthetic pesticides.

economical.note: L. explicitly positions the line as accessible period care that should not stress the user's budget.

ethics.note: L. funds nonprofit period-equity partners, but it is owned by P&G rather than being an independent mission-locked company.

accessibility.note: Brand site points shoppers to Target, Walmart, Walgreens, CVS, and Kroger, making it one of the easiest organic-ish lines to find.

products.description: L. is a high-access organic-cotton mainstream option: easier to buy than boutique brands, but still disposable and corporate-owned.

products.name: Seventh Generation period care

environment.note: Organic cotton and plant-based applicator claims improve the footprint, but tampons and pads are still disposable products.

health.note: Seventh Generation publishes period-care ingredient lists, including cotton tampons and pad component materials.

economical.note: A premium organic disposable line with recurring costs; generally cheaper upfront than reusables but not the lowest per-cycle option.

ethics.note: Seventh Generation has long-standing B Corp and ingredient-disclosure positioning, but is now part of a large multinational portfolio.

accessibility.note: Available through large retail channels such as Walmart, but not as ubiquitous as Always, Tampax, or store brands.

products.description: Seventh Generation is useful as a better-disclosed organic disposable line with mainstream retail access and single-use tradeoffs.

products.name: Grace & Green organic period care

environment.note: Grace & Green combines organic disposable products with zero-waste reusables, but disposable formats still have recurring material impacts.

health.note: B Lab profile says products use organic bamboo and cotton and are free from pesticides, dyes, bleaches, and other toxic chemicals.

economical.note: Mission-led organic products are usually a premium recurring purchase unless the user chooses the reusable range.

ethics.note: B Lab lists Grace & Green as a Certified B Corp with a 146.5 overall B Impact Score and a designed-to-give impact model.

accessibility.note: Strong UK presence and online purchasing, but less available than mainstream US drugstore brands.

products.description: Grace & Green adds a strong UK/EU mission-led option with unusually strong B Corp evidence and both disposable and reusable products.

products.name: Applicator-free tampons (e.g. o.b.)

environment.note: o.b. product page states no applicator waste; tampon itself is still single-use.

health.note: o.b. regular tampons are fragrance-free and elemental-chlorine-free; users still need standard tampon/TSS guidance.

economical.note: Mainstream non-applicator tampons are usually cheaper than premium organic disposables but still recur monthly.

ethics.note: Mainstream corporate product with limited public mission or third-party values certification compared with B Corp period brands.

accessibility.note: Compact and sold through major pharmacies/retailers, though less universal in the US than applicator tampons.

products.description: Applicator-free tampons are a lower-waste mainstream disposable option, though they remain single-use and less mission-led.

products.name: Cardboard-applicator tampons (e.g. Tampax Cardboard)

environment.note: Cardboard applicator avoids plastic applicator waste but the tampon, wrapper, and box remain disposable.

health.note: Tampax Cardboard page states no perfume, dyes, or chlorine bleaching; standard tampon safety guidance still applies.

economical.note: Mainstream disposable pricing is lower upfront than organic disposables and reusables, but recurs every cycle.

ethics.note: P&G mainstream ownership and no period-care mission certification; this is a lower-plastic format rather than a values-led maker.

accessibility.note: Available through major retailers, but plastic-applicator variants remain more common in many stores.

products.description: Cardboard-applicator tampons reduce plastic applicator waste while keeping the familiar mainstream tampon format.

products.name: Always pads

environment.note: Always pads are single-use; Always' materials page lists plastic, cellulose, adhesive, and absorbent components that vary by product.

health.note: Always says most pads are unscented and pad fibers are purified without elemental chlorine bleach; variant-level sensitivity checks still matter.

economical.note: Target lists Always Maxi pads at low per-pad pricing, cheaper upfront than reusables but recurring every cycle.

ethics.note: P&G presents Always as part of a large mainstream brand portfolio rather than a third-party certified or mission-led period-care maker.

accessibility.note: Target lists Always pads with same-day delivery, Drive Up, and order pickup, reflecting very broad mainstream access.

products.description: A highly accessible disposable pad anchor: easy to find and relatively low upfront, with recurring cost and single-use waste tradeoffs.

products.name: Tampax Pearl tampons

environment.note: Tampax Pearl combines a disposable tampon, wrapper, and plastic applicator, so convenience comes with recurring single-use waste.

health.note: Tampax says Pearl uses purified cotton/rayon, no added perfumes, and no elemental chlorine bleaching; standard tampon safety guidance still applies.

economical.note: Target lists common Tampax Pearl packs at low per-tampon pricing, but purchases recur across cycles.

ethics.note: P&G mainstream ownership and no period-care mission certification keep this closer to the conventional anchor than to values-led makers.

accessibility.note: Target carries multiple Tampax Pearl counts and absorbencies online, signaling broad pharmacy and big-box availability.

products.description: The mainstream plastic-applicator tampon benchmark: very easy to buy, moderately transparent on materials, and firmly single-use.

products.name: Kotex Click compact tampons

environment.note: Compact applicators reduce size, but the tampon, plastic applicator, wrapper, and box remain disposable.

health.note: Kotex says Click tampons are OEKO-TEX certified, hypoallergenic, fragrance-free, gynecologist tested, and made with elemental chlorine-free rayon.

economical.note: Target lists Kotex Click around mainstream per-tampon pricing, lower upfront than reusables but recurring every cycle.

ethics.note: Kimberly-Clark lists Kotex among its global essential brands and publishes sustainability topics, but the product is not a mission-led certification play.

accessibility.note: Target lists Kotex Click with online purchase and pickup/delivery options, making it a widely reachable mainstream tampon.

products.description: A mainstream compact-applicator tampon with stronger material disclosure than many conventional options, but still a disposable format.

products.name: Playtex Sport tampons

environment.note: Playtex Sport is a plastic-applicator tampon format; the tampon, applicator, wrapper, and package remain single-use.

health.note: Playtex discloses Sport ingredients including rayon, cotton, waxes, and polymers; fragrance-free variants still require normal tampon safety practices.

economical.note: Target lists Playtex Sport at low per-tampon mainstream pricing, with the usual recurring disposable-product cost.

ethics.note: Essity completed acquisition of global Playtex feminine-care rights in 2026; the brand is mainstream rather than third-party mission certified.

accessibility.note: Target lists Playtex Sport with online purchase and store fulfillment, showing broad access for a conventional tampon brand.

products.description: A sport-positioned conventional tampon anchor: accessible and inexpensive per count, but plastic-applicator and single-use.

products.name: Supermarket own-brand

environment.note: Typical store-brand pads/tampons are single-use, often with plastic applicators, backings, wrappers, or multipack packaging.

health.note: FDA regulates menstrual products, but ingredient/material disclosure is uneven; check unscented and allergy-relevant details product by product.

economical.note: Walmart Equate listings show low per-count pricing relative to premium organic brands.

ethics.note: Retailer/manufacturer ethics vary and are rarely the main selling point for generic period products.

accessibility.note: Low price and same-day pickup/delivery at major retailers make store brands one of the easiest access options.

products.description: Store-brand tampons and pads are often the cheapest and easiest to find, but usually weaker on materials transparency and waste.

products.name: Conventional tampons/pads (mainstream)

environment.note: Carbon Literacy's 2025 summary says disposable pads and tampons generate significant plastic waste and rely on fossil-fuel-derived materials.

health.note: FDA draft guidance covers tampon, pad, and cup testing/labeling; conventional products can be safe when used correctly, but transparency varies.

economical.note: Single-use products are cheap per pack, but current reusable-product comparisons show recurring disposable purchases cost more over years.

ethics.note: Mainstream products usually lack the third-party mission, B Corp, organic, or reusable-waste credentials of higher-scoring alternatives.

accessibility.note: Conventional pads and tampons are the most broadly available formats in pharmacies, supermarkets, schools, and workplaces.

products.description: The mainstream default is easy and cheap up front, but creates repeated waste and offers weaker values signals than reusable or transparent organic options.

products.name: Daye organic tampons

environment.note: Daye says its organic tampons use 100% organic cotton, no plastic in the tampon, sugarcane applicators, and recyclable packaging.

health.note: Daye says its tampons use a no-shed protective sleeve, gamma sanitization, ISO 13485/GMP manufacturing, and published safety testing.

economical.note: Daye positions the product as a premium organic tampon and notes production to stricter safety and sustainability standards raises cost.

ethics.note: B Lab lists Daye Biotech as a Certified B Corp with an overall B Impact Score of 93.6.

accessibility.note: Daye sells directly online and shows country options across the US, UK, and multiple European markets, but it is still less shelf-common than mainstream brands.

products.description: A premium organic tampon line with unusually detailed safety and manufacturing claims, best treated as a values-forward disposable rather than a low-cost default.

products.name: FLO period care

environment.note: FLO has strong plant-based and impact claims, but 2025 reporting noted the brand was removing several pad/liner green claims after a dispute.

health.note: Retail listings describe FLO pads as organic bamboo and non-GMO corn fiber, with hypoallergenic and fragrance-free positioning.

economical.note: FLO is sold through mainstream retailers but remains a premium disposable product rather than a low-cost store-brand option.

ethics.note: B Lab's live profile lists Here We Flo as a Certified B Corporation with a 109.9 B Impact Score and a 5% profits-to-people-and-planet mission.

accessibility.note: Target's current FLO category page lists multiple pads, liners and tampons with pickup, store, same-day delivery and shipping options.

products.description: A highly visible challenger brand with strong social-impact signals, but some environmental language now needs a more cautious read.

products.name: Organic Initiative (Oi) period care

environment.note: Oi says its disposable period products use certified organic cotton, biodegrade over five years under the right conditions, and use recyclable packaging.

health.note: Oi says its organic cotton is grown without toxic sprays or pesticides and that chlorine is not used to bleach the cotton.

economical.note: Oi offers subscriptions and retail availability, but certified organic disposables remain recurring purchases.

ethics.note: Oi emphasizes certified organic materials and a women-designed period-care mission, though no B Corp-style certification was found on its site.

accessibility.note: Oi lists online subscriptions and stockists, but shelf access is narrower than multinational mainstream brands.

products.description: A certified-organic disposable line that improves materials transparency, while still sharing the recurring-waste tradeoff of single-use period care.

products.name: Lena Cup

environment.note: Lena positions its menstrual cup as a reusable alternative that can replace many disposable pads and tampons over years of use.

health.note: Lena lists medical-grade silicone, FDA registration, and BPA-free/latex-free/toxin-free materials for its Sensitive cup.

economical.note: A reusable cup has high upfront but low per-cycle cost when it fits; Lena sells multipacks and replacement-light cup formats.

ethics.note: Lena has clearer materials and manufacturing claims than generic cups, but no B Corp-style governance certification was found.

products.name: WUKA period swimwear

environment.note: WUKA describes its period swimwear as reusable and made with recycled ocean waste, with built-in protection for light-to-medium flow days.

health.note: WUKA publishes PFAS-free claims for its period wear; swimwear still needs to be matched to flow and worn according to instructions.

economical.note: The upfront price is high compared with disposables, but repeated swim use can make the reusable format more sensible than buying single-use backups.

ethics.note: WUKA is a Certified B Corp and has a clearer reusable-period-care mission than many mainstream swimwear sellers.

accessibility.note: WUKA is strongest in UK/EU online access; price, sizing, flow limits, and washing needs keep it less universal than supermarket disposables.

products.description: A values-strong swimwear option for light-to-medium flow or backup use, with better mission signals than most but real upfront cost.

products.name: Knix leakproof swimwear

environment.note: Knix leakproof swimwear is reusable and machine washable, so it can reduce disposable backup dependence when the style and absorbency fit.

health.note: Knix publishes product-testing and safety information, but past PFAS-marketing litigation makes this a more cautious materials-transparency score.

economical.note: Swimwear pricing is high relative to pads or tampons, so value depends on frequent swimming and whether the garment works without extra purchases.

ethics.note: The reusable format helps, but contested PFAS-free marketing claims keep the transparency/ethics score below stronger certified or mission-led brands.

accessibility.note: Knix has mainstream recognition, teen options, size guidance, and US/global online access, making it easier to find than many niche swimwear brands.

products.description: A widely available reusable swim option, scored cautiously because accessibility is stronger than its contested materials-transparency history.

products.name: Ruby Love period swimwear

environment.note: Ruby Love says its period bathing suits are reusable, giving it a waste advantage over single-use swim backups when the garment works.

health.note: Ruby Love describes built-in absorbent liners and optional added protection, but public material/certification detail is thinner than top transparency leaders.

economical.note: The swimwear can be reused and machine washed, but the listed prices are high enough that value depends on repeated use and reliable fit.

ethics.note: The brand offers a specific reusable period-swim category, but public mission, certification, and sourcing evidence is limited.

accessibility.note: Ruby Love sells adult and teen swimwear online, but price, style fit, and the need for backup on heavier flow limit universal access.

products.description: A reusable period-swimwear specialist with adult and teen options; useful for swim access, but weaker on certification depth and price.
